title: What makes an API pleasant to integrate against
description: The traits that let a stranger build against your API without ever emailing you, using invoicelens's first paying integrator as the case study.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the traits that let an integrator build against an API without contacting the API owner
Evaluate whether a specific response design will hold up under automated, unattended use

contentSections.title: The first integrator

contentSections.body: invoicelens has been a web app for a year: someone uploads one invoice, watches a spinner, reads the extracted vendor, total, and line items on screen. Today an accounts-payable automation startup emails: they want to call it programmatically, 400 invoices a night, with no human ever looking at a screen. This is the first customer who will never see your UI — only your JSON.

contentSections.scenario: Two invoice-extraction APIs return the extracted total. API A's response shape depends on the invoice: sometimes `{ total: 412.50 }`, sometimes `{ totalAmount: 412.50 }`, sometimes a nested `{ amounts: { total: 412.50 } }` when the invoice has multiple currencies. API B always returns the same envelope — `{ amounts: { total: number | null, currency: string } }` — with `total: null` when no total was found, never a differently-shaped response.
contentSections.question: The AP startup's pipeline runs unattended overnight with no human reading the output. Which API can they actually build against?

options.label: API A — it's fine as long as the docs explain when each shape appears
API B — the shape is identical on every response, so one parser handles every invoice
Either — a competent integrator will write code that handles all three of A's shapes

feedback.b: Right. An unattended pipeline needs exactly one code path to read the total, every time. API B's `total: null` still tells the integrator something happened (nothing found) without changing the shape their parser has to expect.
feedback.a: Documenting the three shapes doesn't remove the cost of handling them — the integrator's code still needs a branch for each one, and a fourth shape appearing later (a new invoice type) breaks all of it. Documentation describes the inconsistency; it doesn't remove the work of coding around it.
feedback.either: A competent integrator *can* write code that branches on all three shapes of API A, but that's real, ongoing engineering cost paid by every integrator, for every new shape you introduce — cost that API B's callers simply don't pay.

contentSections.concept: **A response shape that depends on the input forces every integrator to reverse-engineer and handle that variation themselves.** A predictable envelope — same keys every time, `null` instead of omission when something isn't found — is what makes unattended, automated use possible at all.

contentSections.body:
Three traits separate an API people can build against from one they can only poke at manually:

1. **Predictable response shape.** The same keys appear on every response for a given endpoint, in the same nesting, whether or not the value was found. Nothing is added or removed based on what happened to be in the input.
2. **Sane defaults.** A first call should work with the smallest reasonable request — one required field, not twelve. Options exist for the cases that need them, but nobody should have to read your source code to make their first successful call.
3. **Errors that don't require a human to interpret.** If something goes wrong, the response says what and, ideally, what to do about it — not a stack trace, not a bare `500`, not silence.

invoicelens's current response for a two-currency invoice nests everything under `amounts`; for a single-currency invoice it flattens `total` to the top level "to keep it simple." That's the inconsistency the AP startup just found in their first hour of integration.
A pleasant API is one where the shape of the response never depends on what happened to be in the request — that's what lets a stranger write one parser instead of a family of special cases.

contentSections.title: The support-ticket predictor

contentSections.body: invoicelens's API beta runs for a month. Forty support emails come in. Thirty-one of them are some version of the same question: "why does `total` say `null` on this invoice — did it not find one, or did parsing fail?"

contentSections.scenario: invoicelens returns `"total": null` in two completely different situations: (1) the invoice genuinely has no total field (a packing slip mistakenly uploaded as an invoice), and (2) the parser found what looked like a total but couldn't confidently extract the number (a total printed as a handwritten figure). Both produce the identical `null`.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism generating a third of a month's support volume around one field?

options.label: The docs don't explain what `null` means — better documentation would fix it
Two genuinely different situations — nothing to find, versus found-but-uncertain — are collapsed into one identical value with no way to tell them apart from the response alone
Integrators should build their own confidence-scoring on top of the raw output instead of relying on invoicelens for it

feedback.collapsed: Right. No amount of documentation fixes this, because the problem isn't that the meaning of `null` is undocumented — it's that one value is being asked to mean two different things. An integrator reading `null` genuinely cannot tell, from the response alone, whether to flag the invoice for a human or move on.
feedback.docs: Documenting that `null` can mean either thing doesn't give the integrator's code anything to branch on — they still can't tell which situation they're in for a specific response, so every `null` has to be treated as the worse case (flag for human review), which is exactly the outcome they were trying to automate away.
feedback.user-error: The confidence question is real, but it's not something integrators can reconstruct from a single collapsed `null` — there's no raw signal left to score. The fix has to happen in the response design, not downstream of it.

contentSections.mechanism: **When a response value has to mean more than one real-world situation, every integrator hits the same wall and asks the same question — that's not scattered confusion, it's one design gap generating identical support tickets.** The fix is a response that keeps the two situations distinguishable: something like `"total": null, "totalStatus": "not_present" | "low_confidence"` instead of one overloaded `null`.

contentSections.body:
The general version of this: before shipping a field, ask what real-world situations could produce the same value, and whether the integrator needs to tell those situations apart. If they do, the field needs enough structure to say which one happened — a `null` plus a status, a confidence score, an explicit `notFound` boolean — not just the bare value and a hope that the docs cover it.

This is also the cheapest place to prevent support volume: a support email is a sign the *response itself* didn't answer a question the integrator was always going to ask. Answering it in the JSON is strictly cheaper than answering it in an inbox, and it scales — the tenth integrator gets the same answer as the first.

An API's job is to answer the integrator's next question before they have to ask it — a support ticket is usually proof that a response value was collapsing two situations an integrator needed told apart.

title: Resource naming, HTTP verbs, and status codes that mean what they say
description: Naming invoicelens's endpoints around resources instead of actions, and choosing status codes an automated caller can actually make decisions on.

learningObjectives.text: Name REST endpoints around resources and let the HTTP verb carry the action
Choose status codes that let an automated caller distinguish retryable, permanent, and successful outcomes

contentSections.title: Naming resources instead of naming actions

contentSections.body: invoicelens's current API surface: `POST /api/parseInvoice`, `POST /api/reparseInvoice`, `GET /api/getInvoiceResult?id=abc123`, `POST /api/deleteInvoice`. Every endpoint is a verb. None of them look like they belong to the same API.

contentSections.question: These four endpoints all work correctly today. What's the actual defect, per REST convention?

options.label: Nothing — each URL clearly says what it does, which is what matters
The action is encoded in the URL instead of the HTTP verb, so there's no consistent pattern an integrator can predict for a resource they haven't seen yet
The camelCase URLs should be kebab-case instead — that's the real issue

feedback.verbs: Right. `parseInvoice`, `reparseInvoice`, `getInvoiceResult`, `deleteInvoice` all describe an action on the same underlying thing — an invoice — but each invents its own verb and its own URL shape. An integrator who's used one endpoint can't predict the next one. REST's alternative: name the resource once (`/invoices`), and let GET/POST/DELETE carry the action, so the pattern generalizes to resources the integrator hasn't touched yet.
feedback.fine: Individually readable isn't the same as predictable as a set. A human can figure out what each endpoint does by reading its name, but an integrator building a client library has to hardcode four unrelated URL patterns instead of inferring one pattern — that's the real cost, and it gets worse as the API grows past four endpoints.
feedback.casing: Casing is a real but minor style question — fixing it to `parse-invoice` wouldn't change the underlying problem, which is that the URL is doing the verb's job.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The REST version: `POST /api/invoices` (create/parse), `GET /api/invoices/:id` (fetch a result), `POST /api/invoices/:id/reparse` (a genuine action on an existing resource, nested rather than invented from scratch), `DELETE /api/invoices/:id`. One noun, four standard verbs, and the pattern now predicts what a fifth endpoint on invoices would look like without needing to be told.

contentSections.body:
### Naming rules, applied to invoicelens

- **Plural nouns for the resource**: `/invoices`, not `/invoice`.
- **No verbs in the URL**: the HTTP verb already means "create" (POST), "read" (GET), "remove" (DELETE) — repeating that in the path is redundant and, worse, becomes a second, inconsistent way of saying the same thing.
- **Nest genuine sub-actions or sub-resources**: `POST /invoices/:id/reparse` is a real action *on* a specific invoice, so it nests under it. This is different from `parseInvoice`, which invented a whole new top-level verb for something that's really "create an invoice resource."
- **Query params for filtering, not for identifying a specific resource**: `GET /invoices/:id`, not `GET /invoices?id=abc123` — the ID is part of *what* you're asking for, not an optional filter on a list.

```
POST   /api/invoices           → submit a new invoice for parsing
GET    /api/invoices/:id       → fetch one invoice's result
POST   /api/invoices/:id/reparse → re-run extraction on an existing invoice
DELETE /api/invoices/:id       → remove an invoice's stored data
GET    /api/invoices           → list invoices (with ?status=, ?since= filters)
```
Name the resource once, let GET/POST/DELETE carry the action — a caller who's learned one endpoint should be able to predict the shape of the next one.

contentSections.title: Status codes that mean what they say

contentSections.body: The AP startup's pipeline hits a corrupted PDF and retries it every ten minutes for two days straight, quietly burning their invoicelens quota, before someone notices. The invoice will never parse — it's not a corrupted file it can retry its way past.

contentSections.scenario: invoicelens returns `200 OK` for every request that reaches the server successfully, including `{ "success": false, "error": "corrupt file, cannot parse" }` for the unparseable PDF. The integrator's retry middleware retries any request whose status code isn't 2xx-with-`success:true` — but it's reading the status code first, and `200` short-circuits the check before the body is even inspected.
contentSections.question: Why does the retry loop never stop, even though the response body clearly says the parse failed?

options.label: The integrator wrote a bad retry client — a well-written one would read the body
The status code is the signal automated systems are built to trust first; `200` says "this succeeded" regardless of what the body says underneath it
invoicelens should have used a polling endpoint instead of a synchronous response

feedback.status-lies: Right. HTTP status codes exist precisely so automated systems can make retry/don't-retry decisions cheaply, without parsing every response body. A `200` is a promise that the request succeeded — using it for a permanent failure breaks that contract for every piece of infrastructure (retry middleware, monitoring, load balancers) built to trust status codes first.
feedback.bad-client: A retry client that trusts status codes over body content isn't badly written — it's following the actual point of HTTP status codes, which is to let infrastructure make decisions without parsing every payload. Blaming the client here just means every one of invoicelens's integrators has to independently discover and work around the same mislabeled response.
feedback.should-poll: Sync vs. polling is a separate design question — either style still needs the status code to say what actually happened. A polling endpoint returning `200` for a permanently-failed job would have exactly the same bug.

contentSections.mechanism: **Automated clients are built to trust the status code before they ever look at the body — that's the entire point of having status codes.** Returning `200` for a failure doesn't just mislabel one response; it breaks every piece of infrastructure downstream that was correctly built to trust HTTP's own contract.

contentSections.body:
### Status codes worth distinguishing for invoicelens

| Code | Means | Retry? |
|---|---|---|
| `201 Created` | Invoice accepted, parsing complete | — |
| `202 Accepted` | Invoice accepted, parsing queued (async) | poll, don't retry POST |
| `400 Bad Request` | Malformed request — missing field, invalid JSON | fix the request, don't retry as-is |
| `401 Unauthorized` | Missing or invalid API key | fix auth, don't retry |
| `402 Payment Required` | Plan's quota or billing is the blocker | not a retry — needs a human |
| `422 Unprocessable Entity` | Request was well-formed, but the file couldn't be parsed (corrupt PDF, unreadable scan) | never retry — it will fail identically forever |
| `429 Too Many Requests` | Rate limit hit | retry after the delay in `Retry-After` |
| `500 Internal Server Error` | invoicelens's own bug | safe to retry once, with backoff |

The distinction that actually mattered in the corrupt-PDF case is `400` vs. `422`: both mean "this didn't work," but `400` means *the request itself* was wrong (fixable by changing the request), while `422` means the request was fine and the *content* is the problem — retrying the identical request will produce the identical failure every time.

A status code is a promise to every piece of automated infrastructure reading it — 200 means succeeded, full stop, and a permanently-unparseable file needs a code that says "stop retrying," not one that says "try again."

title: Versioning a public API without breaking existing integrations
description: What counts as a breaking change, and how invoicelens ships an improvement without waking up 12 integrators' pipelines overnight.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish breaking changes from additive ones in a JSON API response
Choose a versioning strategy and deprecation runway for a change that must break something eventually

contentSections.title: The 2am rename

contentSections.body: invoicelens ships a cleanup: `total` becomes `totalAmount`, with a new separate `currency` field, "to make the money field's name unambiguous." It goes straight to production at 2am, no announcement beyond a one-line changelog entry. By 9am, 12 of invoicelens's 40 integrators have pipelines throwing null-total errors — their code still reads `response.total`, which no longer exists.

contentSections.scenario: invoicelens emails all 40 integrators the moment the rename ships, with a clear subject line: "Breaking change: `total` renamed to `totalAmount`."
contentSections.question: Of the 40 integrators, how many do you guess actually read that email and updated their code before their pipeline broke?
contentSections.explanation: Realistically about 3. Most integrators don't read changelog emails proactively — they find out about a breaking change when their pipeline throws an error, which is exactly what happened to the other 37. A changelog is a record of what happened, not a mechanism that prevents anything from breaking. Anything that must not break needs to be enforced in the API itself — old and new fields coexisting, or a version boundary — not communicated and hoped for.

contentSections.body:
### What actually counts as breaking

- **Removing or renaming a field** — breaking. Any code reading the old name now gets `undefined`.
- **Changing a field's type or meaning** — breaking, even with the same name. If `total` used to be a number and becomes a string, or used to be pre-tax and becomes post-tax, every consumer's assumption is now silently wrong.
- **Changing the default behavior** — breaking. If invoices used to include all line items by default and now only include the first 10 unless `?full=true` is passed, existing callers silently get less data.
- **Adding a new optional field** — *not* breaking. Existing parsers ignore keys they don't recognize.
- **Adding a new endpoint** — not breaking. Nobody's existing code calls it.
- **Loosening a validation rule** (accepting an input that used to be rejected) — not breaking for existing callers, though worth a note for anyone relying on the old rejection.

The test that generalizes: **would code written against the old behavior, unchanged, now do something different or fail?** If yes, it's breaking, no matter how small the diff looks in a pull request.
A changelog documents a breaking change; it doesn't prevent one. Anything that must not break existing integrators needs to be enforced by the API's shape, not communicated and hoped for.

contentSections.title: Choosing a strategy, and a deprecation runway that isn't a cliff

contentSections.body: invoicelens needs to actually make the `total` → `totalAmount` change — the old name really was ambiguous once multi-currency invoices existed. The question isn't whether to change it, it's how to change it without another 2am incident.

contentSections.scenario: Three proposed changes to invoicelens's `/invoices/:id` response: (1) add a new `totalAmount` field alongside the existing `total`, keeping both for now; (2) add a new optional `?includeLineItemImages=true` query parameter; (3) change line items from an unordered array to always being sorted by page number.
contentSections.question: Which of these three is the one that actually requires a version boundary or careful rollout, versus the ones that can ship freely?

options.label: The sort-order change — anything relying on the array's previous order (even implicitly, like taking items[0] as "the first line item as printed") silently gets different results with no error thrown
Adding `totalAmount` alongside `total` — new fields are the riskiest kind of change since old clients don't expect them
The new optional query parameter — any addition to the request shape needs a version bump

feedback.sort-order: Right. This is the one genuinely dangerous change of the three, and it's dangerous precisely because it's silent — no field is renamed or removed, so it won't show up in a naive diff of the response shape, but any integrator relying on array order (even unintentionally) gets different, wrong-looking results with no error to alert them.
feedback.add-field: Adding a field alongside the old one is the textbook non-breaking, additive change — old clients ignore keys they don't recognize, so `total` keeps working exactly as before while `totalAmount` becomes available for anyone who wants it.
feedback.query-param: A new optional query parameter changes nothing for callers who don't pass it — existing requests are unaffected. This is additive, same as the new field, and needs no version boundary.

contentSections.concept: **The riskiest breaking changes are the silent ones — nothing removed, nothing renamed, but behavior that changes anyway.** Sort order, default filtering, rounding behavior, and pagination defaults are the usual suspects: they don't show up in a "what fields changed" review, but they break any consumer that depended on the old behavior without realizing they were depending on it.

contentSections.body:
### A versioning strategy that survives the next change too

**URL path versioning** (`/api/v1/invoices`, `/api/v2/invoices`) is the simplest to support and the easiest for an integrator to reason about — the version is visible in every request and every log line, with no header inspection required to know what a request will do.

For invoicelens's actual rename: ship `totalAmount` as an addition to `v1` first (non-breaking), announce that `total` is deprecated with a target removal date, add a `Deprecation` and `Sunset` response header to every `v1` response still using it, and only remove `total` entirely in `v2` — which existing integrators are never forced onto; `v1` keeps working, deprecated field and all, until they choose to move or the sunset date arrives with fair warning baked into every response they've been receiving.

The sort-order fix from the concept-flow above follows the same shape: ship the sorted order under a new endpoint or version, never silently change the meaning of data an existing version is already returning.
Ship additive changes freely, but changes that alter existing behavior — even silent ones like sort order — need a version boundary and a real deprecation runway, not a changelog entry and a hope.

title: An error contract callers can actually branch on
description: One consistent error envelope across every invoicelens endpoint, and the difference between a stable error code and a human-readable message that's free to change.

learningObjectives.text: Design one consistent error response shape used across every endpoint of an API
Distinguish which parts of an error response are safe for a caller to build branching logic on

contentSections.title: Three endpoints, three different ways to fail

contentSections.body: invoicelens's `/invoices` route returns `{ "error": "missing file" }` on failure. `/invoices/:id/reparse` returns `{ "message": "invoice not found", "code": 404 }`. A request that hits an unhandled exception anywhere else falls through to Express's default handler and returns raw HTML — a stack trace, not JSON at all.

contentSections.question: An integrator writes one error-handling function to wrap all invoicelens calls. What's the actual defect across these three routes?

options.label: There's no single, predictable error shape across the API — different field names, and one route that isn't even JSON — so no single piece of error-handling code can cover all three
The status codes themselves (400, 404) are wrong choices for these situations
Nothing wrong — the integrator just needs three different error handlers, one per route

feedback.no-shared-shape: Right. `error` vs. `message`, a redundant `code` field duplicating the status code, and a route that returns HTML instead of JSON on failure — an integrator has no single place to look for "what went wrong," and the third case will actively crash a JSON parser expecting a consistent response.
feedback.wrong-status: 400 for a missing required field and 404 for a resource that doesn't exist are both reasonable status code choices on their own — the problem isn't the status codes, it's that the JSON body accompanying them has no consistent shape from one route to the next.
feedback.fine: Three error handlers for three routes is exactly the cost this lesson is about — and it gets worse linearly as invoicelens adds routes. One consistent error contract means one error handler, ever, no matter how many endpoints exist.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is one error envelope, used by every route including a catch-all handler for unexpected exceptions: `{ error: { code: 'MISSING_FILE', message: 'The `file` field is required.', details: {} } }` on every failure, everywhere, with the catch-all handler guaranteeing route 3's raw exception gets wrapped in the same shape instead of leaking as HTML.

contentSections.body: One error envelope, produced by one catch-all handler, used by every route — an integrator should never need more than one piece of error-handling code, no matter how many endpoints exist.

contentSections.title: The field that's safe to branch on, and the one that isn't

contentSections.body: An integrator writes `if (err.message.includes('could not find vendor')) { flagForReview(invoice); }` to detect one specific failure mode. Three weeks later invoicelens's copywriter improves the wording to "vendor name could not be determined" for clarity. The integrator's flagging logic silently stops firing — no error, no crash, just invoices that should have been flagged quietly sailing through.

contentSections.scenario: invoicelens's error response includes: an HTTP status code (`422`), a `code` field (`"VENDOR_NOT_FOUND"`), a `message` field (human-readable prose), and a `details.field` value (`"vendor"`) pointing at which extracted field failed.
contentSections.question: Which of these are safe for an integrator to write branching logic against — code that decides what to do next based on that value?

items.label: The HTTP status code (422) — coarse-grained, but a stable contract
The `code` field ("VENDOR_NOT_FOUND") — a stable enum-style identifier
The `message` field — human-readable prose meant to be read, not matched against
`details.field` ("vendor") — a stable, structured pointer at what failed

explanation.status: Status codes are part of HTTP's own stable contract — 422 will always mean "well-formed request, unprocessable content," and changing that meaning would break far more than one API.
explanation.error-code: This is exactly what a `code` field like `VENDOR_NOT_FOUND` is for — an identifier that's contractually stable, documented, and safe to build a switch statement against, precisely because it's understood to be an API contract rather than UI copy.
explanation.message: Prose is understood, by convention, to be free to reword for clarity, translation, or tone — that's what broke the integrator's flagging logic. Nothing in an API contract promises message text won't change; only the `code` field carries that promise.
explanation.details-field: A structured field like `details.field: "vendor"` is designed to be read programmatically — it names which extracted field the error concerns, in a fixed vocabulary, which is exactly the kind of value safe to switch on.

contentSections.synthesis: **The dividing line isn't "is this text or a code" — it's "did the API promise this value won't change."** Status codes and dedicated `code`/`details` fields are the contract; `message` is customer-facing prose that's supposed to be free to improve. Document which is which, and integrators stop building on the wrong one.

contentSections.body: Document the `code` field as a closed, stable enum — `MISSING_FILE`, `VENDOR_NOT_FOUND`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `QUOTA_EXCEEDED`, and so on — and commit to never changing an existing code's meaning, only adding new ones. `message` is explicitly *not* part of the contract: state that outright in the docs, so nobody has a reason to build logic against wording that a copywriter is free to improve next week. This single distinction — one field that's a promise, one that's prose — is what let invoicelens improve its error wording without silently breaking every integrator who'd written string-matching logic against the old phrasing.
A `code` field is a promise; a `message` field is prose free to improve. Say so explicitly in the docs, and integrators stop building fragile logic against wording that was never meant to be stable.

title: Documenting an endpoint so a stranger can use it without asking you
description: What a doc actually needs to answer on its own, and how invoicelens keeps its examples from drifting away from what the API really returns.

learningObjectives.text: Assemble endpoint documentation that answers a real integrator's actual first questions
Design a process that keeps documentation examples matching what the API actually returns

contentSections.title: What a doc actually needs to answer

contentSections.body: invoicelens has docs. Three separate integrators, in three separate weeks, email the same question anyway: "what does the `confidence` field actually mean?" The docs mention `confidence` exists. They never say what the number means or what a caller should do differently at 0.4 versus 0.9.

contentSections.intro: Assemble the documentation for invoicelens's `GET /invoices/:id` endpoint from the pieces below, choosing the version of each piece that would actually stop a stranger from needing to email you.

options.label: "confidence: how confident the parser was in the result"

"confidence: a 0–1 score per extracted field. Below 0.6, treat the value as needing human review before use — invoicelens's own accuracy testing shows values above 0.6 are correct 98% of the time, below it, roughly 70%."
Omit a definition — the field name is self-explanatory

feedback.concrete: This is what actually stops the emails — it tells the integrator not just what the number represents but what to *do* with it, with a concrete threshold backed by a real number, not a restatement of the field's name.
feedback.vague: This just repeats the field name in slightly more words — it doesn't tell an integrator what value should trigger different behavior in their pipeline, which is the actual question all three emails were asking.
feedback.omit: "Self-explanatory" is exactly what led to three separate emails asking the same question — a number with no defined meaning or threshold isn't actionable on its own.

fields.prompt: What should the example response in the docs be?

options.label: { vendor: string, total: number, confidence: number } — the TypeScript-style shape
A real, complete response captured from an actual invoicelens call, including a field that came back null, so an integrator can see what that looks like
The smallest possible valid response, to keep the doc short

feedback.real-recorded: A real captured example shows the shape *and* what an edge case (a null field) actually looks like in practice — an integrator can copy it directly into a test fixture and know it reflects reality, not an idealized type signature.
feedback.typed-placeholder: A type signature tells you the shape but not what real values look like, and it hides exactly the edge cases (a null total, a low confidence, an empty line-items array) that integrators most need to see before they hit them in production.
feedback.minimal: The smallest valid response is also the least representative one — it's unlikely to include the fields and edge cases (nulls, low confidence, multi-currency) that actually cause confusion.

fields.prompt: How should errors for this endpoint be documented?

options.label: A general note: "errors are returned as JSON with a code and message"
Every specific `code` this endpoint can return, each with the situation that produces it and the HTTP status that comes with it
Skip error documentation — the code field names are self-explanatory

feedback.full-list: This is what lets an integrator write complete error handling *before* they've hit every error in production — a full enumerated list, not a general description of the shape.
feedback.generic: This describes the envelope, not the actual set of things that can go wrong — an integrator still has to discover each specific error code by triggering it themselves.
feedback.skip: Even a well-named code like `VENDOR_NOT_FOUND` doesn't tell an integrator what situation produces it or what status code accompanies it — that has to be documented, not inferred from the name.

contentSections.synthesis: A doc that stops the emails has three things the vague version lacked: a definition that says what to *do* with a value, not just what it's called; a real captured example including edge cases, not an idealized type signature; and a complete, specific list of error codes rather than a description of the error shape in general. Each of these turns a question an integrator would otherwise have to email in for into something they can answer themselves, in the doc, in under a minute.

contentSections.body: A doc that stops the emails answers what a value means to *do with*, shows a real captured example including edge cases, and lists every specific error — not a description of the shape errors come in.

contentSections.title: Keeping the docs honest

contentSections.body: A month after the `total` → `totalAmount` rename ships, the docs' example response still shows `total`. Nobody updated it during the rename PR — the docs live in a separate repo nobody thought to touch.

contentSections.question: Put these practices in the order that most effectively prevents documentation from drifting away from what the API actually returns — starting with the practice that catches drift earliest.
steps: Docs live in the same repository and the same pull request as the API code they describe, so a route change and its doc update are reviewed together
Example responses in the docs are generated from a real, current API call rather than hand-typed
An automated test runs the documented example requests against the real API and fails the build if the actual response no longer matches what's documented
Integrators report drift they notice, and it gets fixed in the next docs update
contentSections.explanation: The first three practices catch drift before it ships at all — same PR means a reviewer sees the mismatch immediately, generated-from-real-calls means there's no hand-typed example to go stale in the first place, and an automated test catches anything that slips through both of those as a genuine build failure. Waiting for integrators to report drift is the practice invoicelens was actually relying on, and it's the slowest and most expensive one: by the time a report arrives, an unknown number of other integrators have already read the wrong example and possibly built against it.

contentSections.body: Treat documentation drift as a bug, not a chore — because that's what it functionally is: incorrect information an integrator will act on. The concrete version of "same PR, generated example, automated test" for invoicelens: a small script that hits the real `/invoices/:id` endpoint against a fixture invoice, captures the response, and writes it directly into the docs file as part of CI; if the API's shape changes and nobody updates the doc-generation script accordingly, the generated example changes automatically and the diff makes the change visible in code review — nobody has to remember to touch the docs by hand, and there's no chance of an example silently going stale.

Documentation drift is a bug, not a chore — generate examples from real API calls in CI so a shape change makes the doc change automatically, instead of relying on someone remembering to update a separate file by hand.

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Eight drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here expires — do them in one sitting or spread across a few.

title: Design and document one chargeable endpoint for your tool
description: Take one real endpoint from your own tool and give it the resource naming, status codes, error contract, versioning note, and documentation a paying integrator could build against without emailing you.

learningObjectives.text: Design one real endpoint's request/response contract and error cases from scratch
Self-assess an endpoint spec against an explicit rubric before calling it done

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every filter from this module — resource naming over verbs-in-URLs, status codes automated callers can act on, a versioning plan for the change you know is coming, one consistent error envelope, docs that answer the actual question instead of restating the field name — is easiest to prove on a real endpoint from a real tool, not a hypothetical one. This lab designs and documents exactly one chargeable endpoint from your own tool, the way this module designed invoicelens's `/invoices/:id`.

contentSections.title: Design one endpoint a stranger could integrate without asking you anything
contentSections.brief: Pick one real endpoint from a tool you're building or maintaining — the one most likely to be worth charging for. You're not building the whole API. You're designing and documenting this one endpoint completely enough that a stranger, reading only what you produce here, could integrate against it and never need to email you.
contentSections.deliverable: An endpoint spec with request/response examples, error cases, and versioning note

stages.title: Name it and choose its contract
stages.instructions: Write the endpoint's method and path, following resource-noun naming (no verbs in the URL). List every status code it can return and the specific situation each one represents — including at least one case where a permanent failure (never worth retrying) is distinguished from a transient one (worth retrying).
stages.checkpoint: The endpoint has a resource-based path, and its status codes distinguish retryable from permanent failures.

stages.title: Write the request/response examples and error cases
stages.instructions: Write one complete, realistic example request and response — real-looking values, not type placeholders, including at least one field that can legitimately come back null or empty so a caller can see what that looks like. Then write the full error contract: one consistent envelope shape, and every specific error code this endpoint can return with the situation that produces it.
stages.checkpoint: A real example exists showing at least one edge-case value, and every error this endpoint can return is listed with its code, situation, and status.

stages.title: Add a versioning note and write the doc
stages.instructions: Write one sentence naming the change to this endpoint you consider most likely in the next six months, and whether it would be breaking or additive by this module's test. If breaking, sketch the deprecation runway (what ships first, what signal warns callers, how long the runway is). Then assemble the actual one-page doc a stranger would read: method+path, auth, the request/response example, and the full error list.
stages.checkpoint: A likely future change is named and classified as breaking or additive, and a complete one-page doc exists that a stranger could act on without further questions.

rubric.criterion: The endpoint is named around a resource, not an action
rubric.meets: The path uses a plural noun for the resource and lets the HTTP verb carry the action — no verb appears in the URL itself.

rubric.criterion: Status codes distinguish retryable from permanent failures
rubric.meets: At least one status code is used for a failure that will never resolve on retry, and it's different from the code used for a transient failure.

rubric.criterion: The response shape doesn't depend on the input
rubric.meets: The same keys appear in every example response for this endpoint; a missing or not-found value is represented as null or an explicit status, never by omitting the key.

rubric.criterion: The error contract is one consistent envelope with real, specific codes
rubric.meets: Every listed error uses the same JSON shape, and each has a real, specific `code` value plus the situation that produces it — not a generic description of the shape errors come in.

rubric.criterion: The doc answers real integrator questions without needing to be asked
rubric.meets: A stranger reading only the doc could write working request code and complete error handling without emailing the author.

contentSections.body: The real test of an endpoint spec isn't whether it looks complete to you — it's whether a stranger who has never spoken to you could integrate against it and never need to.

title: Checkpoint — An API Worth Paying For
description: Ten questions, all from this module — it's the first module of the phase, so there's nothing earlier to pull from yet. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — An API Worth Paying For
contentSections.framing: Ten questions pulled from this module. Nothing graded, nothing timed — this is just a look at what's stuck so far.

questions.from: This module — An API Worth Paying For
questions.prompt: invoicelens's response shape changes depending on whether an invoice has one currency or several. What's the actual cost to an integrator running an unattended pipeline?

options.label: None — most invoices are single-currency, so most callers are unaffected
Every caller has to branch on which shape they received, on every response, forever
It only matters if the integrator's code is poorly written

questions.explanation: The branch has to run on every response regardless of how rare the alternate shape is, because the caller can't know in advance which shape is coming.

questions.from: This module — An API Worth Paying For
questions.prompt: invoicelens's `confidence` field is one number covering the whole invoice, and integrators can't tell which extracted field it's actually warning about. What's the fix?

options.label: Attach a confidence score per extracted field, not one blended number for the document
Remove the confidence field entirely — it's causing more confusion than it's worth
Round the confidence number to fewer decimal places

questions.explanation: A single blended number was collapsing several independent judgments (about vendor, total, date, etc.) into one value with no way to tell which extraction it's actually about.

questions.from: This module — An API Worth Paying For
questions.prompt: Which pair of invoicelens endpoints follows REST naming convention correctly?

options.label: POST /api/parseInvoice and POST /api/deleteInvoice
POST /api/invoices and DELETE /api/invoices/:id
POST /api/invoices/create and POST /api/invoices/remove

questions.explanation: The resource (invoices) is named once; the HTTP verb (POST, DELETE) carries the action, instead of the URL inventing its own verb.

questions.from: This module — An API Worth Paying For
questions.prompt: invoicelens returns 200 OK with `{ success: false }` for a permanently corrupt PDF, and an integrator's retry logic loops forever. What's the actual mechanism behind the infinite retries?

options.label: Automated clients trust the status code first; 200 tells all of them the request succeeded, regardless of the body
The integrator's retry client is simply buggy
invoicelens should have used a slower response time to signal failure

questions.explanation: Retry infrastructure is built to make cheap decisions off the status code before parsing the body — a 200 breaks that contract regardless of what the body underneath it says.

questions.from: This module — An API Worth Paying For
questions.prompt: What distinguishes a 400 response from a 422 response for invoicelens?

options.label: 400 means the request itself was malformed and fixable; 422 means the request was fine but the content can never be processed as-is
They're interchangeable — both mean "something went wrong"
400 is for server bugs, 422 is for client bugs

questions.explanation: The distinction is retryability: fixing a 400 means changing the request; a 422 (like a genuinely corrupt PDF) will fail identically no matter how many times the identical request is retried.

questions.from: This module — An API Worth Paying For
questions.prompt: invoicelens renames `total` to `totalAmount` and emails all integrators the same day. Roughly how many actually update their code before their pipeline breaks, and what does that imply?

options.label: Nearly all of them — a clear changelog email is usually enough warning
A small minority — a changelog documents a change but doesn't prevent it; the API itself has to enforce backward compatibility
Exactly half — email open rates are typically around 50%

questions.explanation: Most integrators only discover a breaking change when their pipeline throws an error, not by reading a changelog — anything that must not break needs to be enforced structurally (old and new fields coexisting), not communicated and hoped for.

questions.from: This module — An API Worth Paying For
questions.prompt: invoicelens changes line items from an unordered array to always sorted by page number, without renaming any field. Why is this still a breaking change?

options.label: It isn't breaking — no field was renamed or removed
Any caller relying on the array's previous order, even unintentionally, silently gets different results with no error thrown
It's only breaking if the array has more than 10 items

questions.explanation: This is the silent category of breaking change — sort order, default filters, rounding — that doesn't show up in a shape diff but changes what existing callers actually receive.

questions.from: This module — An API Worth Paying For
questions.prompt: An integrator writes code that checks `err.message.includes('vendor not found')`. invoicelens rewords the message for clarity, and the integrator's logic silently stops working. What should the integrator have branched on instead?

options.label: A stable, documented `code` field like `VENDOR_NOT_FOUND`, not the human-readable message text
The exact same message string, just cached locally in case it changes
The response's Content-Length header

questions.explanation: A `code` field is documented as a stable contract; `message` is prose that's explicitly free to change for clarity or translation.

questions.from: This module — An API Worth Paying For
questions.prompt: Three integrators separately email invoicelens asking what the `confidence` field means, despite it being mentioned in the docs. What was actually missing from the documentation?

options.label: A concrete definition of what the number means and what threshold should trigger different behavior — not just that the field exists
A longer field name than `confidence`
Nothing — some integrators just don't read docs carefully

questions.explanation: Mentioning a field exists isn't the same as documenting what to do with its value — the fix was a concrete definition with an actionable threshold, not a restatement of the field's name.

questions.from: This module — An API Worth Paying For
questions.prompt: A month after a field rename ships, invoicelens's docs still show an example response with the old field name. What process change would have caught this before it shipped?

options.label: Generating the example response from a real API call as part of CI, so a shape change makes the doc change automatically and visible in the same pull request
Adding a reminder to the team's calendar to check the docs quarterly
Asking integrators to report drift when they notice it

questions.explanation: Generating examples from real calls in CI catches drift at the moment it's introduced, in the same review as the code change — waiting for integrators to notice is the slowest and most expensive way to catch it.

title: Why you almost never touch a card number yourself
description: What PCI compliance actually costs a solo developer, and why invoicelens routes every card number straight to a payments provider instead of its own server.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what PCI DSS compliance requires and why a solo developer avoids taking it on directly
Identify where card data flows in a hosted-checkout integration and why it never touches your own server

contentSections.title: The form that looks simple and isn't

contentSections.body: invoicelens is ready to charge for API access. The obvious-looking plan: add a form with card number, expiry, and CVC fields, POST them to your own `/api/charge` endpoint, and call a payments API from there. It's four input fields. It looks like an afternoon of work.

contentSections.scenario: PCI DSS (the card industry's security standard) applies to any server that stores, processes, or transmits raw card numbers — even just receiving them in a POST body before forwarding them onward counts.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many individual security requirements does the simplest PCI compliance tier (for a business handling card data directly, even briefly) actually involve — firewall rules, encryption standards, access logging, and so on?
contentSections.explanation: The lightest self-assessment tier (SAQ A-EP, for merchants whose own server touches card data even in transit) runs to roughly 78 individual controls: specific firewall configurations, encryption-at-rest and in-transit rules, access logging and review cadence, quarterly vulnerability scans, and more — audited, not just self-certified in the easy cases. This is the real cost hiding behind "it's just four input fields": the fields aren't the hard part, being the server those fields' values pass through is.

contentSections.body:
The moment a card number reaches your server — even for a single millisecond before you forward it to a payments API — your server is now "in scope" for PCI DSS. That triggers real, ongoing obligations: network segmentation, specific encryption requirements for data at rest and in transit, quarterly vulnerability scans, access logging, and in some tiers, an actual external audit. None of this is optional once card data touches your infrastructure, and none of it is a one-time cost — it's an ongoing compliance burden for as long as the card form exists.

The alternative almost every solo developer and small team actually uses: never let the card number reach your server at all. A hosted checkout page or an embedded widget from a payments provider (Stripe, Paddle, and similar) collects the card details directly, on infrastructure that's already fully PCI-compliant at a scale your solo project will never need to replicate. Your server only ever sees a token — a reference the payments provider hands back — never the number itself.
The moment a card number reaches your server, your server is in scope for PCI DSS — the fix isn't handling it carefully, it's never letting it arrive in the first place.

contentSections.title: What a breach actually costs, versus what avoiding it costs

contentSections.body: A developer on a forum argues: "I'll just hash and encrypt the card numbers myself, like I do with passwords. How different can it be?" invoicelens's founder has to decide whether that instinct is reasonable.

contentSections.scenario: Password hashing (bcrypt, a salt, one-way) is a well-understood, one-time engineering task a solo developer can genuinely get right. A developer proposes the same instinct for card numbers: encrypt them at rest with a strong algorithm, keep the key separate, done.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that makes this comparison misleading?

options.label: Encryption algorithms for card data are fundamentally weaker than bcrypt

A password only ever needs to be *verified* (one-way, hash-and-compare); a card number needs to be *reversible and reusable* to actually charge the card later, which is a different, much harder problem with legal liability attached if it goes wrong
It's purely a regulatory technicality — the actual engineering risk is comparable to password storage

feedback.different-shape: Right. A password hash never needs to be turned back into the original password — one-way is exactly what you want. A stored card number has to be recoverable enough to actually charge the card again (a subscription renewal, for instance), which means it can't be irreversibly hashed the way a password can, and now you're maintaining a reversible secret with regulatory liability if it leaks — a fundamentally different, harder problem than password storage, not a bigger version of the same one.
feedback.encryption-weak: The math isn't the weak point — competent encryption exists for both cases. The mismatch is in the requirement itself: passwords need one-way verification, card numbers need reversible reuse, and that difference is what makes "just encrypt it like a password" the wrong mental model from the start.
feedback.regulatory-only: The legal liability is real, but it's downstream of a genuine engineering difference, not the whole story on its own — even setting PCI aside, building and maintaining a reversible-secret storage system correctly is a much larger and higher-stakes task than hashing passwords, which is exactly why a provider that already does it at scale is worth the fee.

contentSections.mechanism: **"I already handle sensitive data carefully" doesn't transfer from passwords to card numbers, because the two have opposite requirements — one-way verification versus reversible reuse — and the reversible case carries regulatory liability the one-way case never does.** This is why "how different can it be" undersells the actual gap: it's not a harder version of the same problem, it's a different problem wearing similar words.

contentSections.body: This is also why the payments provider's fee (typically ~2.9% + a fixed amount per transaction) isn't really a fee for "processing a payment" — it's a fee for taking on PCI scope, fraud detection, chargeback handling, and 3D Secure authentication entirely on their infrastructure, none of which a solo developer building invoicelens could build more cheaply, faster, or more safely alone. The fee buys out a category of risk, not a feature.
A payments provider's fee isn't for moving money — it's for taking on PCI scope, fraud detection, and chargeback handling that would cost far more, in both money and risk, to build yourself.

title: Checkout flow: what happens between click and confirmed payment
description: Tracing invoicelens's actual checkout flow from "Subscribe" click to a confirmed Pro-plan account, and where the payments provider hands control back.

learningObjectives.text: Trace the full sequence of a hosted-checkout payment flow from click to confirmed state
Identify which step in that sequence is the one your own server actually controls

contentSections.title: Three ways to charge, and why invoicelens starts with the middle one

contentSections.body: invoicelens's founder researches payment integration and finds three very different-looking options: a shareable payment link generated in a dashboard with zero code, a hosted checkout page with a small integration, and a fully custom card form embedded in invoicelens's own pricing page. All three end with the same money in the same account.

contentSections.scenario: Option A: a Stripe-hosted Payment Link, created entirely in a dashboard, shared as a URL — zero code. Option B: Stripe Checkout, a hosted page invoicelens redirects users to, created via a small backend call. Option C: Stripe Elements, a fully custom card form embedded directly in invoicelens's own pricing page, giving complete control over styling.
contentSections.question: invoicelens needs to attach a specific plan (Pro vs. Team) and a specific user ID to each payment, and eventually wants a polished on-brand checkout. Which option should it start with?

options.label: Option B (Checkout) — enough control to attach metadata like plan and user ID, without taking on the UI and validation work of a fully custom form yet
Option A (Payment Link) — zero code is always the right place to start
Option C (Elements) — go straight for full control since polish matters eventually

feedback.b: Right. Checkout gives invoicelens exactly what it actually needs right now — the ability to pass metadata like which plan and which user this payment is for — through a small, well-tested integration, without taking on the real cost of Option C: building and maintaining a card form's validation, error states, and security posture by hand.
feedback.a: A Payment Link is genuinely zero code, but it also can't easily attach per-user metadata like which invoicelens account should be upgraded — invoicelens would have to build a separate reconciliation step to figure out who paid, which is more total work than starting with Checkout.
feedback.c: Full styling control is a real eventual want, not a day-one need — Elements means invoicelens takes on building its own validation, error handling, and 3D Secure UI, which Checkout already handles for free. Reaching for it before the simpler option has been outgrown is the same over-engineering-too-early pattern from other modules, applied to payments.

contentSections.concept: **Match the integration to what you actually need right now: metadata attachment matters for invoicelens today, custom styling doesn't yet.** Checkout gives the former without the cost of the latter — start there, and reach for a fully custom form only once Checkout's constraints genuinely become the bottleneck.

contentSections.body: Start with hosted Checkout, not a fully custom form — it gives you metadata attachment and a polished, secure flow for free, and a custom form is worth its real cost only once Checkout's limits are the actual bottleneck.

contentSections.title: Where your server's control actually starts and stops

contentSections.body: invoicelens's frontend redirects a user to Stripe's page, and the user is gone — for anywhere from ten seconds to, in one real case, four days (they closed the tab and came back to finish later). invoicelens's own server has no visibility into anything happening during that gap.

contentSections.question: Put the steps of an invoicelens Pro subscription checkout in the actual order they happen.
steps: User clicks "Subscribe to Pro"; invoicelens's backend creates a Checkout session with the user's ID in metadata
invoicelens's frontend redirects the browser to the session's hosted URL on Stripe's domain
The user enters card details and completes payment entirely on Stripe's page — invoicelens's server has no visibility into this step
Stripe redirects the browser back to invoicelens's success_url
Stripe separately sends a checkout.session.completed webhook to invoicelens's server
invoicelens's webhook handler reads the metadata, finds the user ID, and upgrades that account to Pro in the database
contentSections.explanation: The redirect to `success_url` and the webhook are two separate, independent things happening around the same time — not one causing the other. The success_url redirect is for the *user's browser*; the webhook is for *your server*, and it's the webhook, not the redirect, that actually triggers the database update, which the next lesson goes into directly.

contentSections.body: The gap between step 2 and step 4 is real, and it's the part every naive integration gets wrong: your server has no idea what's happening on Stripe's page. The user could complete payment in ten seconds, abandon the tab entirely, or come back four days later to finish. Your server can't watch any of that happen — it can only find out *afterward*, through one specific mechanism, which is where the next lesson picks up.
Between the redirect to Stripe and the redirect back, your server has zero visibility — it isn't watching the payment happen, it's waiting to be told afterward.

title: Webhooks: why payment confirmation can't live only in the redirect
description: Why invoicelens's account upgrade has to happen in a signature-verified webhook handler, not in the success_url redirect — and what breaks when it doesn't.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a webhook, not the success redirect, is the trustworthy signal that a payment actually completed
Implement a webhook handler that verifies its signature before acting on the event

contentSections.title: The upgrade that happened without a payment

contentSections.body: An early version of invoicelens upgrades a user to Pro the moment their browser lands back on `/account?checkout=success` — no other check. A curious user notices they can navigate to that exact URL directly, with no payment at all, and gets Pro for free.

contentSections.scenario: invoicelens's `success_url` handler runs: `if (req.query.checkout === 'success') { await upgradeToProPlan(req.user.id); }` — triggered purely by the browser landing on that URL with that query parameter.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that let a user get Pro for free, and what does it reveal about trusting the redirect?

options.label: The query parameter name ("success") was too easy to guess — a random token would fix it
The redirect is controlled entirely by the user's own browser — it's a UI convenience Stripe provides, not a signal your server can trust as proof that money actually moved
The endpoint wasn't using HTTPS, so the parameter could be tampered with in transit

feedback.redirect-not-proof: Right. Nothing about a browser landing on a URL with a specific query string proves a payment happened — the browser is fully under the user's control, and anyone can type or construct that URL directly. Stripe's redirect is a UI nicety ("send the user back here when they're done"), not a cryptographically verifiable claim your server can trust.
feedback.url-guessable: A random token in the URL is still just something the user's browser possesses and can replay or, in some flows, construct — it doesn't change the underlying problem, which is that nothing about landing on a URL is proof that a real payment was verified server-to-server.
feedback.needs-https: HTTPS protects data in transit from being intercepted or tampered with by a third party — it does nothing to stop the actual user, who legitimately controls their own browser, from simply navigating to a URL they already know.

contentSections.mechanism: **Anything driven purely by where the user's browser ends up is information the user controls, not proof of anything your server should trust.** A webhook, by contrast, is a server-to-server call from Stripe directly, carrying a cryptographic signature your server can verify — proof the event actually came from Stripe, not from a browser doing whatever a browser can do.

contentSections.body: The fix is a strict separation of responsibilities: `success_url` is *only* for what the human sees — a "Payment received, setting up your account" message, nothing more. The actual account upgrade happens exclusively inside a webhook handler, triggered by a server-to-server event from Stripe that your code cryptographically verifies before acting on it. If the webhook hasn't fired yet when the user lands on the success page, the UI can say "finishing up" and poll or refresh — but nothing about granting access should ever depend on which URL the browser happens to be sitting on.
The success_url redirect is for what the human sees — never for what your server trusts. A browser landing on a URL is user-controlled information, not proof a payment happened.

contentSections.title: Verifying the webhook is actually from Stripe

contentSections.body: invoicelens builds the webhook handler correctly this time — except it doesn't check where the POST request actually came from. A month later, someone finds the webhook URL in invoicelens's public API docs and POSTs a fake `checkout.session.completed` event directly, granting themselves Pro for free.

contentSections.question: Why does Stripe verify webhooks with a cryptographic signature instead of just having invoicelens check that the request came from one of Stripe's published IP address ranges?
contentSections.answer: **IP allowlisting is both weaker and higher-maintenance.** Stripe's outbound IP ranges can change, requests may pass through load balancers or proxies that alter the apparent source address, and an IP address alone proves nothing about whether the specific payload was tampered with in transit. A signature computed from a shared secret over the exact request body proves both origin and integrity — it wouldn't matter if an attacker somehow spoofed a Stripe IP, they still couldn't produce a valid signature without the secret.
contentSections.hint: Think about what an IP address actually proves versus what a cryptographic signature proves — and what happens to an IP-based check the day Stripe adds a new data center.

contentSections.body: A webhook endpoint is a public URL anyone can POST to — signature verification, not the shape of the payload, is what actually proves an event came from Stripe.

title: Handling failed payments, disputes, and refunds without losing the customer
description: invoicelens's response to a declined card, a chargeback, and a refund request — three different failure modes needing three different handlers, not one generic error path.

learningObjectives.text: Design distinct handling for a failed payment, a dispute, and a refund based on what each situation actually needs
Implement a webhook handler that reacts to a subscription's payment_failed event without immediately cutting off access

contentSections.title: A declined card isn't a canceled subscription

contentSections.body: invoicelens's Pro-plan renewal runs monthly. A customer's card expired without them noticing. The renewal charge fails. invoicelens's webhook handler, written to only ever grant access on success, does nothing on failure — so nothing happens: no notice sent, no retry, and the customer's access silently keeps working until, eventually, Stripe gives up retrying and cancels the subscription outright, at which point access vanishes with zero warning.

contentSections.question: What's the actual defect here, given that a renewal charge just failed on an expired card?

options.label: There's no handling at all for a failed renewal — no warning to the customer, and access is later cut off abruptly with no notice, instead of a graceful "update your card" grace period
The bug is that access isn't revoked immediately the moment the charge fails
Stripe should be configured to never retry a failed charge, since retries are the actual source of confusion

feedback.no-response: Right. The gap isn't too much leniency or too little — it's total silence. A customer whose card simply expired (extremely common, not fraud, not intent to cancel) gets no notification to fix it and no warning before access disappears; the first they hear of it is when invoicelens stops working, with no context.
feedback.should-cancel-immediately: Cutting access immediately on the first failed charge would punish the most common, most innocent cause — an expired card — the same as deliberate non-payment, and would generate exactly the kind of angry, avoidable churn this lesson is about preventing.
feedback.stripe-should-retry: Stripe's automatic retry schedule (commonly over about two weeks) is actually the useful part — it's the *silence* around those retries, not the retries themselves, that's the problem. Removing retries would make the situation worse, not better.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is a dedicated `invoice.payment_failed` handler: email the customer that their card was declined and why (if Stripe provides a decline reason), keep their access active through Stripe's retry window, and only downgrade access on the separate `customer.subscription.deleted` event that fires once retries are truly exhausted — giving a real, communicated grace period instead of silent access followed by a silent cutoff.

contentSections.body: A failed charge and a canceled subscription are two different events answering two different questions — silence on the first one, followed by sudden access loss on the second, is what turns an expired card into an angry customer.

contentSections.title: A dispute isn't a refund request

contentSections.body: A customer emails invoicelens asking for a refund on a Pro subscription they forgot to cancel. Separately, a different customer's bank files a chargeback dispute on a charge they claim they never authorized. invoicelens's founder, in a hurry, handles both the same way: refund the money and move on.

contentSections.scenario: Two situations: (1) a customer politely emails asking for a refund, having simply forgotten to cancel; (2) a customer's *bank* files a formal dispute (chargeback) claiming the charge was unauthorized, which comes through Stripe as a `charge.dispute.created` event with a response deadline.
contentSections.question: Which of these characteristics apply to the dispute (situation 2) but not the plain refund request (situation 1)?

items.label: There's a hard deadline to respond with evidence, or the dispute is automatically lost
invoicelens is typically charged a dispute fee by the payment processor regardless of the outcome
Money leaves invoicelens's account either way
invoicelens's own support team can simply resolve it by clicking a button in the dashboard, no different from processing a refund

explanation.deadline: A dispute has a formal response window (commonly around a week to a few weeks depending on the card network) — missing it means automatically losing the dispute regardless of the facts, which is not true of an ordinary refund request that can be handled whenever.
explanation.fee: Card networks charge the merchant a dispute fee (often in the $15 range) simply for a dispute being filed, win or lose — an ordinary refund carries no such fee, since it's a voluntary transaction reversal rather than a formal bank-initiated challenge.
explanation.money-moves: This is true of both — a straightforward refund and a lost or accepted dispute both result in the customer getting their money back. It doesn't distinguish the two situations from each other.
explanation.reversible-by-support: A refund genuinely can be a one-click action in a support workflow. A dispute cannot — it requires actually submitting evidence (proof of the service being delivered, terms accepted, usage logs) to the card network within the deadline, or it's lost by default regardless of whether invoicelens was in the right.

contentSections.synthesis: A refund is invoicelens choosing, voluntarily, to give money back. A dispute is the customer's *bank* formally challenging the charge, with a real deadline and a real fee attached regardless of outcome — treating the two identically means dispute deadlines get missed by teams who think "we'll just refund it" is always available, when for a genuine chargeback, evidence and a timely response are what's actually required.

contentSections.body: The practical difference for invoicelens: a refund request gets handled through Stripe's refund API whenever it's convenient, no urgency. A `charge.dispute.created` webhook needs a process with a deadline built in — someone actually checks it, gathers evidence (the invoice the customer downloaded, their account's API usage logs showing the service was used, the terms they agreed to), and submits it through Stripe before the response window closes. Missing that window means losing automatically, dispute fee included, even when invoicelens was clearly in the right — which is a very different cost than the small, voluntary cost of an ordinary refund.
A refund is your own voluntary choice; a dispute is the customer's bank formally challenging the charge with a real deadline and fee — treat them as the same thing and the deadline gets missed.

title: Keeping payment secrets out of your codebase and logs
description: Where invoicelens's Stripe secret key and webhook secret actually belong, and the quiet ways a secret leaks even when nobody commits it to git on purpose.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the places a payment secret can leak beyond an obvious git commit
Design a logging and error-handling approach that never writes secret values or full card numbers to a log

contentSections.title: The leak that wasn't a git commit

contentSections.body: invoicelens's founder is careful — the Stripe secret key lives in an environment variable, never committed to git, exactly as the docs recommend. Months later, a routine review of the error-tracking dashboard turns up the full secret key, in plain text, inside a logged stack trace from a crashed request.

contentSections.scenario: A bug in invoicelens's checkout code throws an exception that includes the full request object in its error message, which the error-tracking tool logs verbatim, including the `Authorization: Bearer <STRIPE_SECRET_KEY>` header the Stripe SDK had attached internally to its outbound request.
contentSections.question: How did a secret that was never committed to git end up sitting in a monitoring dashboard anyway?

options.label: This is a bug in the Stripe SDK exposing secrets it shouldn't
Generic error/request logging captured everything about the failing request — including headers a library had attached — without anyone deciding that headers specifically should be excluded
Environment variables are inherently insecure and shouldn't be used for secrets at all

feedback.logging-swept-it-up: Right. "Never committed to git" only protects against one specific leak path. A secret can still leak through anything that logs a request or an error verbatim — and a generic "log everything about the failure to help debug it" instinct will happily sweep up an Authorization header along with the rest, because nothing was ever configured to treat that header as sensitive.
feedback.sdk-bug: The SDK attached the header exactly where it's supposed to, for exactly its intended purpose (authenticating the outbound API call) — the leak happened downstream, in invoicelens's own logging, which captured more of the request than it should have.
feedback.env-var-insecure: Environment variables are the right place for this secret to live at rest — the leak didn't happen because the variable was insecurely stored, it happened because something else (verbose error logging) captured and persisted the value elsewhere, in a place with weaker access controls than the env var itself.

contentSections.mechanism: **Keeping a secret out of git only closes one leak path — anything that logs a request, an error, or a response verbatim is a separate path the same secret can travel through, entirely independent of version control.** "Never committed" and "never logged" are two different disciplines, and most teams only build the first one on purpose.

contentSections.body: Keeping a secret out of git closes one leak path — verbose error and request logging is a separate one, and it needs its own redaction rule, applied to every request, not left to individual code paths remembering not to log something.

contentSections.title: What a webhook handler should never write to a log

contentSections.body: Debugging a subscription bug, invoicelens's founder adds `console.log(event)` to the webhook handler to see what's coming through — a completely reasonable debugging instinct. The full Stripe event object, including the customer's last-four card digits, billing address, and email, now lands in invoicelens's server logs, retained for 90 days by the hosting provider's default log retention.

contentSections.question: Besides the `authorization` header, what's another value flowing through invoicelens's own requests that belongs on the same proactive redaction list, before it ever shows up in a bug report?
contentSections.answer: **Session cookies and any custom API-key header invoicelens's own users authenticate with** (for instance, the `Authorization: Bearer` header its own API customers send). The same logic that leaked the Stripe secret key applies to invoicelens's own auth material — anything that proves someone's identity or grants access is worth redacting by default, not just the payments provider's secrets.
contentSections.hint: The Stripe key wasn't the only thing capable of authenticating a request in invoicelens's system — what does invoicelens's own API use to authenticate its customers?

contentSections.body:
The last-four digits of a card aren't the full card number, and by themselves they're not PCI-scoped data — but combined with a name, billing address, and email in the same log line, they're a real piece of a customer's financial identity sitting in a system (general server logs) that almost never has the same access controls, encryption, or retention discipline as a payments provider's own dashboard, where that same information is actually meant to live.

The practical rule for invoicelens's webhook handler: log the event *type* and the *ID* freely (`checkout.session.completed`, `evt_1a2b3c`) — those are safe, useful for debugging, and contain nothing sensitive. Never log the full `event.data.object` verbatim. If a specific field is genuinely needed for debugging, pull out only that field by name:

```js
logger.info('Processing webhook', { type: event.type, id: event.id }); // safe
// NOT: logger.info('Processing webhook', event); — logs everything, including PII
```

Stripe's own dashboard already keeps a full, searchable log of every event, encrypted and access-controlled to the standard PCI requires — there's rarely a real debugging need to duplicate that data into a general-purpose server log with weaker protection.

Log the event type and ID freely — they're safe and enough to debug with. Never log a full webhook payload verbatim; it carries customer PII into a system with weaker protection than the payments provider's own dashboard already gives it.

title: Diagnose seven broken payment integrations

Identify the specific broken assumption in a payment integration, not just that something feels risky

title: Wire up a payment provider's checkout and webhook for a test product
description: Build a real, working test-mode checkout and signature-verified webhook handler that correctly updates order state — the actual mechanism this module has been building toward.

learningObjectives.text: Implement a hosted checkout flow that attaches identifying metadata to the payment
Implement a signature-verified webhook handler that correctly updates state based on the event, not the redirect

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every filter from this module — never touching a card number directly, treating the redirect as UI-only, verifying webhook signatures, distinguishing failure types, keeping secrets out of logs — is easiest to prove by actually wiring one up, in test mode, end to end. This lab builds a real checkout and webhook handler for one test product, the way this module built invoicelens's.

contentSections.title: Build a working test-mode checkout and webhook
contentSections.brief: Using a payments provider's test mode (no real money moves), build one product or plan's checkout flow end to end: a backend route that creates a checkout session with identifying metadata, and a webhook handler that verifies its signature and updates your own order or account state based on the event — not the redirect.
contentSections.deliverable: A working test-mode checkout with a webhook handler that updates order state correctly
