contentSections.body: invoicelens's actual implementation: a daily job computes each account's trailing 14-day average OCR spend, compares it against that day's actual spend, and sends a Slack alert — with the account ID, the day's spend, and the baseline — for anything over 2.5×. The alert doesn't touch the account automatically. A human looks, and *then* decides: reach out to the customer (often the fastest fix — most runaway bugs are the customer's own retry loop, and they want it fixed as much as invoicelens does), or in a repeat or clearly malicious case, apply a temporary rate limit specifically to that account while the conversation happens.

A cost threshold that adapts to your own growing baseline catches real anomalies at any scale; the right first response is informing a human, not acting automatically on a customer's account, since a false positive there costs a real relationship.

title: Degrading gracefully instead of falling over entirely
description: invoicelens's OCR provider goes down for two hours — and the choice between a total outage and a smaller, honest degradation turns out to be a design decision, not an accident.

learningObjectives.text: Design a fallback behavior for a dependency failure that preserves partial function instead of total failure
Evaluate when degrading gracefully is the right response versus when failing clearly is better than a confusing partial success

contentSections.title: One dependency down, and everything else went down with it

contentSections.body: invoicelens's OCR provider has a two-hour outage. During those two hours, invoicelens's entire API returns 500 errors for every request — including requests to `GET /invoices/:id`, which only reads already-parsed results from invoicelens's own database and never touches the OCR provider at all.

contentSections.scenario: invoicelens's request-handling code wraps the whole request lifecycle in error middleware that treats any unhandled exception, anywhere in the stack, the same way — including an exception thrown deep inside the OCR client that a completely unrelated read-only endpoint happens to import (but never calls) at module load time, which fails at startup and takes the whole process down.
contentSections.question: Why did a read-only endpoint that never calls the OCR provider still go down during the outage?

options.label: Something in the OCR provider's failure (likely a connection-check at process startup, or a shared module that fails to initialize) took down the entire process, not just the code path that actually depends on it
The database was also down at the same time, coincidentally
This is expected — any dependency outage should reasonably take down an entire API

feedback.coupled-failure: Right. The read endpoint's actual code path never touches the OCR provider — for it to fail too, something at a level above individual request handling (process startup, a shared initialization step, or overly broad error-handling middleware) must be coupling every endpoint's fate to one dependency's health, even when a specific endpoint's real code has no relationship to that dependency at all.
feedback.database-down-too: Nothing in the scenario suggests a coincidental second outage — the far more direct explanation, consistent with what's described, is that one dependency's failure is somehow taking down the whole process rather than being isolated to the code paths that actually use it.
feedback.expected: It's expected that *code paths which actually call* a failing dependency will fail — it is not inevitable that unrelated code paths fail too. That coupling is a specific, fixable architectural choice, not a law of nature.

contentSections.mechanism: **When one dependency's failure takes down code that never calls it, the failure isn't really about that dependency — it's about accidental coupling somewhere in how the system starts up or handles errors, binding unrelated functionality's fate to one component's health.** The fix is architectural: isolate the failure to the code paths that actually depend on the failing thing.

contentSections.body: The concrete fix for invoicelens: the OCR client shouldn't be constructed or health-checked at process startup in a way that can crash the whole app if it's unreachable — it should fail lazily, only when a request that actually needs it calls it. And the error-handling middleware shouldn't treat every exception identically; an exception from the OCR client specifically should produce a clear `503 Service Unavailable` for the *specific* upload/parse endpoints that depend on it, while every other endpoint — reading existing results, checking account status, viewing usage — keeps working exactly as before, because nothing about their actual code depends on the OCR provider being reachable.

A dependency failure should only break the code paths that actually depend on it — if an unrelated endpoint goes down too, the real bug is accidental coupling somewhere in startup or error handling, not the dependency itself.

contentSections.title: When degrading gracefully is the wrong call

contentSections.body: Fixing the coupling, a developer goes further: during an OCR outage, `POST /invoices` should still accept the upload and return `202 Accepted` immediately, queuing the file to parse "whenever the OCR provider comes back" — so the endpoint never has to return an error at all.

contentSections.question: An integrator's automated pipeline receives a 202 Accepted for an upload during a two-hour OCR outage, with no bounded processing time and no status-check endpoint. What does their pipeline actually know, versus what the 202 implied?
contentSections.answer: **It knows almost nothing true.** The 202 implied "this is being handled, proceed" — but the pipeline has no way to know whether the invoice is still queued, silently failed, or will ever be processed at all. If their downstream logic assumes success and moves on (exactly what a 202 tells an automated caller to do), a stuck invoice can go unnoticed for as long as the outage lasts, or longer if the queued job itself fails silently later.
contentSections.hint: Recall this phase's very first module: a status code is a promise to every piece of automated infrastructure reading it. What promise does 202 actually make here, and is it true?

contentSections.body:
This sounds like graceful degradation, and it's actually the wrong move here, for a reason worth naming precisely: **degrading gracefully means preserving real, honest partial function — it does not mean hiding a failure behind a response that looks like success.** `202 Accepted` tells the integrator's automated pipeline "this is being handled, proceed" — but if the OCR outage lasts hours, or the queued job silently fails later, the integrator has no idea their invoice is stuck, because the response they got told them everything was fine.

The honest version: return `503 Service Unavailable` with a `Retry-After` header and a clear error message — "invoice parsing is temporarily unavailable, retry after 300 seconds" — for the endpoint that genuinely can't do its job right now. That's not a worse user experience than a silent, indefinite queue; it's a *truthful* one, and it's the version an automated integrator's pipeline can actually build correct retry logic against, the same lesson this phase's very first module taught about status codes an automated caller can act on.

The cases where returning `202` genuinely would be graceful degradation: a queue with a bounded, predictable processing time the caller is told about upfront, and a way for the caller to check status and find out definitively if it failed — not an open-ended promise dressed up as a completed action.

Graceful degradation means preserving real partial function, not hiding a failure behind a response shaped like success — a 202 that quietly might never resolve is worse than an honest 503, because it breaks the same automated-caller trust this whole phase has been building toward.

title: Triage seven 'it broke under load' incidents
description: Seven drills applying this module's filters — bottleneck tracing, rate limiting, cache-key safety, cost thresholds, and graceful degradation — to invoicelens situations you haven't seen in the lessons.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's scaling filters to unfamiliar incident scenarios at speed
Identify the specific broken assumption behind a scaling failure, not just that something feels overloaded

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here expires — do them in one sitting or spread across a few.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Add rate limiting and a cost alert to your tool
description: Build real, working rate limiting on one endpoint and a genuine cost-alert threshold for your own tool, with a documented reason for the number you chose.

learningObjectives.text: Implement rate limiting scoped to the correct identity, with headers a caller can plan around
Design and justify a cost-alert threshold based on a real baseline for one real cost driver

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every filter from this module — finding the real bottleneck, rate-limiting the right identity, caching only what a precise key can safely identify, and a cost threshold that adapts to your own baseline — is easiest to prove by actually building one real piece of it. This lab adds working rate limiting to one endpoint and a real, justified cost-alert threshold to your own tool.

contentSections.title: Rate-limit one endpoint, and set a cost alert you can defend
contentSections.brief: Pick one endpoint in your own tool that's expensive or abusable — one that calls a paid API, does real computation, or touches a resource with a hard limit. You're not rebuilding your whole infrastructure. You're adding real, working rate limiting to that one endpoint, and setting one real cost-alert threshold for whatever actually costs money as your tool scales, with a documented reason for the specific number you chose.
contentSections.deliverable: Working rate limiting on one endpoint plus a documented cost-alert threshold and why you picked it

stages.title: Identify the real constraint and the right identity
stages.instructions: Trace your chosen endpoint's actual request path and name the real bottleneck it depends on (a third-party API's limit, a database's connection pool, compute cost). Decide what identity the rate limit should be scoped to for your tool — API key, user ID, or something else — and justify why that's more precise than IP address for your specific case.
stages.checkpoint: The real constraint is named specifically, and the rate-limit identity is justified against your tool's actual authentication model.

stages.title: Implement the rate limit with real headers
stages.instructions: Implement working rate limiting on the chosen endpoint, keyed on the identity you justified. Add rate-limit headers to every response — success and failure — not just the one that fails. Test that the limit actually triggers and that a caller could plan around the headers.
stages.checkpoint: The rate limit demonstrably triggers under test, and every response (not just the 429) carries limit and remaining-count information.

stages.title: Set and document a real cost threshold
stages.instructions: Identify your tool's actual biggest real, ongoing cost driver (an API bill, compute cost, storage). Establish a real or estimated baseline for it, and set a threshold based on that baseline — not a round guessed number. Write down, in one paragraph, why you picked that specific threshold and what should happen when it fires (notify vs. automatic action), applying this module's reasoning about false positives.
stages.checkpoint: A specific threshold exists, tied to a real baseline rather than a guess, with a written justification for both the number and the response it triggers.

rubric.criterion: The rate limit targets the actual identity that matters
rubric.meets: The limit is scoped to something more precise than raw IP address where the tool has a more precise identity available (API key, user ID), with a stated reason.

rubric.criterion: Rate-limit headers appear on every response, not just failures
rubric.meets: A successful response carries the same limit/remaining information a caller would need to self-regulate before hitting a 429.

rubric.criterion: The cost threshold is based on a real baseline, not a guessed round number
rubric.meets: The threshold is derived from an actual or realistically estimated cost baseline for the tool, with the derivation shown, not just stated.

rubric.criterion: The response to a threshold breach is justified, not assumed
rubric.meets: A written justification explains why the chosen response (notify vs. automatic action) fits the risk of a false positive for this specific tool.

rubric.criterion: The real bottleneck was actually identified before building anything
rubric.meets: The lab names the specific constraint (a dependency's limit, a resource's capacity) the rate limit or cost alert is protecting, not a generic 'more traffic is bad' justification.

contentSections.body: The real test of a rate limit or a cost alert isn't whether it exists — it's whether the threshold and the identity it's scoped to were chosen for a documented, specific reason, not guessed.

title: Checkpoint — Staying Up When It Works
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous module, two from two modules back. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Staying Up When It Works
contentSections.framing: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the last one, two from further back. Nothing graded, nothing timed.

questions.from: This module — Staying Up When It Works
questions.prompt: invoicelens's web server handles a traffic spike fine, but requests still time out because of a third-party OCR provider's rate limit. What does this reveal about finding a real bottleneck?

options.label: The real bottleneck is the lowest-capacity link in the actual request path, often a downstream dependency, not the layer that's easiest to scale
The web server should have been scaled even further
This means the traffic spike wasn't genuine

questions.explanation: Scaling the web tier changed nothing because it was never the constraint — the OCR provider's fixed limit was.

questions.from: This module — Staying Up When It Works
questions.prompt: 400 distinct, legitimate accounts each making a small number of requests cause a slowdown. What's the correct fix?

options.label: Capacity or queuing fixes — rate-limiting a specific account wouldn't help since no account is individually unusual
Rate-limit the accounts making the most requests
Block traffic from new signups temporarily

questions.explanation: This is an aggregate capacity problem, not concentrated abuse — the fix has to address the aggregate flow, not single out any specific account.

questions.from: This module — Staying Up When It Works
questions.prompt: invoicelens's rate limit is keyed by IP address, unfairly throttling a large customer behind a shared corporate proxy. What's the fix?

options.label: Key the limit by API key, the precise identity already present on every authenticated request
Raise the IP-based limit for everyone
Ask the customer to route traffic differently

questions.explanation: The API key is a more precise identity than IP address for an authenticated API, and doesn't conflate unrelated callers sharing a network.

questions.from: This module — Staying Up When It Works
questions.prompt: Why is a cache keyed on a userId, storing the latest parse result, unsafe compared to a cache keyed on a content hash?

options.label: userId doesn't determine the actual result (file content does), so a genuinely different upload can collide with and mask a stale, wrong cached entry
userId-based caches are always slower to look up
Caching by content hash uses less storage

questions.explanation: A cache key must identify everything that determines the correct result and nothing broader — file content determines a parse result, not who uploaded it.

questions.from: One module back — Analytics Worth Looking At
questions.prompt: invoicelens's dashboard shows rising signups the same month MRR falls. What does this reveal?

options.label: None of the tracked numbers measure whether existing paying users are staying — they're all top-of-funnel volume
The metrics must be mismeasured
MRR always lags other metrics by a month

questions.explanation: Volume metrics and health metrics answer different questions — growth in one can mask decline in the other.

questions.from: One module back — Analytics Worth Looking At
questions.prompt: 90% of invoicelens signups never activate, but retention and revenue look healthy. What's the highest-leverage fix?

options.label: Activation — retention and revenue are only measurable for the small population that already cleared it
Pricing, since revenue matters most
More marketing spend

questions.explanation: Fix activation before retention before revenue, since each is only measurable for users who survived the step before it.

questions.from: One module back — Analytics Worth Looking At
questions.prompt: invoicelens logs 40 million granular events but still can't explain a cancellation. What's the actual problem?

options.label: None of the events were chosen to answer a specific question — quantity isn't the same as signal
The analytics tool is inadequate
Storage cost is the main issue

questions.explanation: A dozen deliberately chosen events answer more than millions logged without being tied to a real product question.

questions.from: One module back — Analytics Worth Looking At
questions.prompt: "That number is still high" repeated for three months never changed anything about invoicelens's product. What was missing?

options.label: A falsifiable hypothesis — a specific change, a specific target number, and a specific window to check it
A bigger dashboard with more charts
